steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting GRANDE, a method for learning decision tree ensembles on tabular data with end-to-end gradient descent. Motivate why tabular data is hard for deep learning, explain how we build on GradTree, and list our contributions and evaluation.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Tabular data: importance, challenges, and the deep learning vs. tree-based gap
- Advantages of gradient-based training and the need for tabular-specific methods
- GradTree and our method GRANDE
- Why hard, axis-aligned trees help; instance-wise weighting
- Contributions and evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Tabular data
  - heterogeneous tabular data most frequently used form of data
  - applications: medical diagnosis, creditworthiness estimation, fraud detection
  - better performance/robustness -> advantages for users and companies
  - challenges: noise, missing values, class imbalance, mixed feature types (categorical, numerical)
  - DL still struggles; XGBoost and CatBoost outperform in most cases
- Gradient-based training
  - end-to-end gradient training has advantages over traditional ML
  - flexibility: arbitrary differentiable losses, iterative training
  - easy to include in multimodal learning
  - tabular-specific gradient methods: active field, strong need
- GradTree -> GRANDE
  - GradTree: gradient descent for hard, axis-aligned DTs; dense representation, backpropagation with straight-through (ST) operator
  - combines tree inductive bias with gradient-based flexibility
  - GRANDE (GRAdieNt-Based Decision Tree Ensembles): end-to-end gradient descent for tree ensembles
  - dense split representation + ST operator; individual trees -> weighted ensemble, efficient computation
- Why it helps
  - DL biased towards smooth solutions; tabular targets usually not smooth
  - hard, axis-aligned DTs learn piece-wise constant functions, no such bias
  - unlike NODE (soft, oblique splits)
  - instance-wise weighting: simple and complex rules in one model; better performance; better local interpretability
- Contributions
  - extend GradTree to tree ensemble (Section 3.1)
  - softsign as differentiable split function (Section 3.2)
  - instance-wise estimator importance weighting (Section 3.3)
  - evaluation: 19 binary classification tasks, predefined tabular benchmark (Section 4)
  - outperforms for default and optimized hyperparameters; large gains on several datasets

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Heterogeneous tabular data is the most frequently used form of data and it is indispensable in many applications such as medical diagnosis, estimating creditworthiness and fraud detection. So improving the predictive performance and robustness of models can give significant advantages to users and companies. But tabular data has considerable challenges like noise, missing values, class imbalance, and a mix of different feature types, especially categorical and numerical data. Deep learning (DL) has been successful in many domains, but recent studies show that tabular data is still a major challenge and tree-based models like XGBoost and CatBoost outperform DL in most cases. At the same time, end-to-end gradient-based training has several advantages over traditional machine learning methods. These methods are very flexible, since they make it easy to integrate arbitrary, differentiable loss functions tailored to specific problems, and they support iterative training. Also, gradient-based methods can be easily used in multimodal learning, where tabular data is one of several input types. So creating tabular-specific, gradient-based methods is a very active research field and there is a strong need for methods that perform well.

- GradTree (prior work)
  - gradient descent for hard, axis-aligned decision trees (DTs)
  - dense representation, joint optimization via backpropagation with straight-through (ST) operator
  - tree inductive bias + flexibility of gradient-based optimization
- Our approach: GRANDE
  - GRAdieNt-Based Decision Tree Ensembles; end-to-end gradient descent for tree ensembles
  - dense split representation and ST operator as in GradTree
  - from individual trees to weighted tree ensemble, still efficient
- Advantage
  - DL biased to smooth solutions, tabular targets usually not smooth
  - hard, axis-aligned DTs learn piece-wise constant functions; NODE uses soft and oblique splits
  - instance-wise weighting: simple and complex rules in one model, better ensemble performance, better local interpretability
- Contributions
  - GradTree extended to ensemble (Section 3.1); softsign split function (Section 3.2); instance-wise weighting (Section 3.3)
  - 19 binary classification tasks on predefined tabular benchmark (Section 4); best for default and optimized hyperparameters

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Heterogeneous tabular data is the most frequently used form of data and it is indispensable in many applications such as medical diagnosis, estimating creditworthiness and fraud detection. So improving the predictive performance and robustness of models can give significant advantages to users and companies. But tabular data has considerable challenges like noise, missing values, class imbalance, and a mix of different feature types, especially categorical and numerical data. Deep learning (DL) has been successful in many domains, but recent studies show that tabular data is still a major challenge and tree-based models like XGBoost and CatBoost outperform DL in most cases. At the same time, end-to-end gradient-based training has several advantages over traditional machine learning methods. These methods are very flexible, since they make it easy to integrate arbitrary, differentiable loss functions tailored to specific problems, and they support iterative training. Also, gradient-based methods can be easily used in multimodal learning, where tabular data is one of several input types. So creating tabular-specific, gradient-based methods is a very active research field and there is a strong need for methods that perform well.

Recently, prior work introduced GradTree, a new approach that uses gradient descent to learn hard, axis-aligned decision trees (DTs). They do this by reformulating DTs into a dense representation and optimizing all tree parameters jointly with backpropagation using a straight-through (ST) operator. Learning hard, axis-aligned DTs with gradient descent lets us combine the good inductive bias of tree-based methods with the flexibility of gradient-based optimization. In this paper we propose GRANDE, GRAdieNt-Based Decision Tree Ensembles, a new approach for learning decision tree ensembles with end-to-end gradient descent. Like GradTree, we use a dense representation for split nodes and the ST operator to handle the non-differentiable nature of DTs. We build on their approach and go from individual trees to a weighted tree ensemble, while keeping the computation efficient. Because of this, GRANDE has a significant advantage over existing gradient-based methods. DL methods are typically biased towards smooth solutions. Since the target function in tabular datasets is usually not smooth, DL methods have trouble finding these irregular functions. Models based on hard, axis aligned DTs, on the other hand, learn piece-wise constant functions and so do not have this bias. GRANDE has this important advantage inherently, because it uses hard, axis-aligned DTs. This is a big difference from existing DL methods for hierarchical representations like NODE, which use soft and oblique splits. We also introduce instance-wise weighting in GRANDE. This lets one model learn appropriate representations for both simple and complex rules, which increases the performance of the ensemble. We also show that our instance-wise weighting has a positive effect on local interpretability compared to other state-of-the-art methods. Our contributions are:

- We extend GradTree from individual trees to an end-to-end gradient-based tree ensemble, while keeping computation efficient (Section 3.1).

- We introduce softsign as a differentiable split function and show its advantage over commonly used alternatives (Section 3.2).

- We propose a new weighting technique that emphasizes instance-wise estimator importance (Section 3.3).

We run an extensive evaluation on 19 binary classification tasks (Section 4) based on the predefined tabular benchmark proposed by prior work. GRANDE outperforms existing methods with both default and optimized hyperparameters. On several datasets the performance difference to other methods is substantial, which makes GRANDE an important extension to the existing set of methods for tabular data.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Heterogeneous tabular data is the most frequently used form of data [1,2] and is indispensable in a wide range of applications such as medical diagnosis [3,4], estimation of creditworthiness [5] and fraud detection [6]. Therefore, enhancing the predictive performance and robustness of models can bring significant advantages to users and companies [7]. However, tabular data comes with considerable challenges like noise, missing values, class imbalance, and a combination of different feature types, especially categorical and numerical data. Despite the success of deep learning (DL) in various domains, recent studies indicate that tabular data still poses a major challenge, and tree-based models like XGBoost and CatBoost outperform DL in most cases [7,8,2]. At the same time, end-to-end gradient-based training offers several advantages over traditional machine learning methods [7]. Such methods are highly flexible, allowing easy integration of arbitrary, differentiable loss functions tailored towards specific problems, and support iterative training [9]. Moreover, gradient-based methods can easily be incorporated into multimodal learning, with tabular data being one of several input types [10,11]. Creating tabular-specific, gradient-based methods is therefore a very active field of research, and the need for well-performing methods is intense [8].

Recently, [12] introduced GradTree, a novel approach that uses gradient descent to learn hard, axis-aligned decision trees (DTs). This is achieved by reformulating DTs into a dense representation and jointly optimizing all tree parameters using backpropagation with a straight-through (ST) operator. Learning hard, axis-aligned DTs with gradient descent combines the advantageous inductive bias of tree-based methods with the flexibility of gradient-based optimization. In this paper, we propose GRANDE, GRAdieNt-Based Decision Tree Ensembles, a novel approach for learning decision tree ensembles using end-to-end gradient descent. Similar to [12], we use a dense representation for split nodes and the ST operator to deal with the non-differentiable nature of DTs. We build upon their approach, moving from individual trees to a weighted tree ensemble while maintaining efficient computation. As a result, GRANDE holds a significant advantage over existing gradient-based methods. DL methods are typically biased towards smooth solutions [13]. As the target function in tabular datasets is usually not smooth, DL methods struggle to find these irregular functions. In contrast, models based on hard, axis-aligned DTs learn piece-wise constant functions and therefore do not show such a bias [8]. This important advantage is inherent to GRANDE, as it uses hard, axis-aligned DTs, and is a major difference to existing DL methods for hierarchical representations like NODE, which use soft and oblique splits [14]. Furthermore, we introduce instance-wise weighting in GRANDE. This allows learning appropriate representations for simple and complex rules within a single model, which increases the performance of the ensemble. We also show that our instance-wise weighting has a positive impact on local interpretability relative to other state-of-the-art methods. More specifically, our contributions are as follows:

- We extend GradTree [12] from individual trees to an end-to-end gradient-based tree ensemble, maintaining efficient computation (Section 3.1).

- We introduce softsign as a differentiable split function and show its advantage over commonly used alternatives (Section 3.2).

- We propose a novel weighting technique that emphasizes instance-wise estimator importance (Section 3.3).

We conduct an extensive evaluation on 19 binary classification tasks (Section 4) based on the predefined tabular benchmark proposed by [15]. GRANDE outperforms existing methods with both default and optimized hyperparameters. The performance difference to other methods is substantial on several datasets, making GRANDE an important extension to the existing repertoire of methods for tabular data.
